frames.narration: A connection starts with a handshake: SYN (client SYN_SENT), SYN-ACK (server was in LISTEN, now SYN_RCVD), ACK. Both sides are then ESTABLISHED.
The client closes first. It sends FIN and goes FIN_WAIT_1, then FIN_WAIT_2 when the ACK arrives. The server is now in CLOSE_WAIT: it has seen the FIN and waits for its application to call close().
The server app closes: FIN, LAST_ACK, then CLOSED once the client ACKs. The client, the active closer, lingers in TIME_WAIT for 60 seconds (typically on Linux) and the port stays reserved.

One client IP to one server address and port can vary only its source port: 28,232 of them. At 400 new connections per second it holds 24,000 in TIME_WAIT and everything works. The ceiling is about 470 per second.

At 600 per second the client needs 36,000 ports. The table pins at 28,232 and new connects fail with 'cannot assign requested address': 15,536 failures in two minutes. Making the server close first moves the TIME_WAIT entries to the server and stops the failures; pooling connections or adding a source IP does too.

Now a server bug. On the error path the app never calls close(), so each such connection sits in CLOSE_WAIT holding a file descriptor. At 2 leaks per 100 requests it is invisible at first, then at tick 500 the 1,024 descriptor limit is hit and the server cannot accept anything.

Last, the accept queue. A burst of 30 connections every third tick against a queue of 8 loses 154 connections. A queue of 32 absorbs every burst when the app accepts 10 per tick. If the app accepts only 5 per tick, even 32 slots drop 88: a bigger queue cannot fix a slower consumer.
